title: I Don't Want Them to Resent Me
author: Chiarelli, Andrea
source: The Art of Asking Questions (theartofaskingquestions.com), September 13, 2026
summary: This piece addresses a fear common among managers moving into senior leadership: that being direct or holding a firm standard will make them seem harsh or cause their team to resent them. Using a composite manager, 'Gemma,' who softens feedback to avoid conflict, the author argues the fear has the causality backwards, since teams actually lose trust in leaders who let standards slide, not in leaders who are consistently honest. Five concrete habits are offered: setting expectations before work starts so later feedback isn't a surprise, being warm to the person while staying honest about the work itself, treating boundaries as something done for the team's benefit rather than against it, knowing when a struggle reflects a genuine skill gap versus mere discomfort, and defending the team's workload and deadlines with senior stakeholders rather than letting unrealistic pressure flow straight through to the team. The piece is candid that this approach doesn't always work, and some people who have been managed loosely for years will resent being held to a new standard and leave, but argues this is evidence the team is course-correcting toward the people who actually fit what it needs.
points: The core reframe: the fear that directness causes resentment has the causality backwards — teams lose trust in leaders who let standards slide, not in leaders who are consistently honest.
Setting clear expectations before work starts removes most of the sting from later feedback, since correction can point back to something both parties already agreed on.
A specific phrase models holding warmth and honesty simultaneously: 'I hold you in high regard, and this piece isn't at the standard we need yet.'
Boundaries are reframed as something done for the team's benefit, not against it — a manager's tolerance for missed deadlines or excuses sets the culture's actual floor.

Defending the team's workload and deadlines with senior stakeholders is named as the most-overlooked habit: a manager who avoids that upward conversation doesn't eliminate the pressure, they just let it flow downward onto the team.
quotes: Serena Spink was recently speaking to a manager (let's call her Gemma) who told her she was worried being assertive would make her sound like a jerk.
But if I come down harder on the team, I'm worried they'll resent me, and I don't want that either.
If nobody agreed what 'done' looked like, or when it was needed, or to what standard, then any correction coming later will feel like a very unpleasant surprise.
You can hold both at once: "I hold you in high regard, and this piece isn't at the standard we need yet.
Your tolerance sets the floor of your team culture, so whatever you allow, you endorse.
A manager who avoids that conversation still leaves the pressure somewhere: it just moves downward onto the team.
In the end, high-performing teams don't want warm leaders who let things slide. They want leaders whose word means something, because that's what makes the job survivable for everyone.
